results.content:
[19:21] And the final verdict? The feed-forward output of InfiniSplat Splat V2 achieves the lowest mean L-pips and the lowest mean DISTS, among all evaluated baselines in both settings.
[19:33] The visual quality is simply unparalleled by current feed-forward standards. state of the art across the board. But as with all papers, there are always physical boundaries to what the math can achieve.
[19:43] What are the explicit limitations of this architecture? Where does it still struggle based on the author's own findings?
[19:49] The authors are very transparent about the hard limits. First, because the architecture relies heavily on pixel-aligned prediction from the input images, it inherently produces some redundancy in the point cloud. Right. [...] [2:37] and previous models try to fix the final rendered image by jointly optimizing both the physical point positions in 3D space and the Gaussian attributes simultaneously, isn't that just a recipe for disaster? It absolutely is.
[2:49] I mean, it feels like trying to fix a terrible peeling paint job on a house by knocking down and physically moving the structural walls.
[2:56] That is a highly accurate way to frame the failure mechanism, honestly.
[3:00] The authors of InfiniSplat Splat V2 found exactly that. The identify this joint optimization process as the root cause of what they term geometric degradation.
[3:09] You have to think about what the loss function is actually doing. The network is receiving image reconstruction supervision. [...] [5:10] Okay, what is it? The geometry branch, the part of the network responsible for predicting the depth maps and the camera poses, is completely frozen during training. Hard locked. Hard locked.
[5:23] Only the attribute branch, which predicts the opacity, the 3D scale the rotation of the color is trainable.
[5:29] The Gaussian centers are fixed permanently at their initial back projected point positions. So the network is physically prevented from moving the coordinates to cheat their reconstruction loss. Exactly.
[5:41] Hold on, I see a glaring issue with this approach. If you lock the geometry, your camera poses and depth maps better be perfectly accurate from the very first step.

results.title: InfiniSplat Moves from Single-Image to Multi-View 3DGS Reconstruction - KIRI Engine
results.content:
Built on Depth Anything 3, InfiniSplat v2 addresses a problem with converting predicted geometry into renderable Gaussians: point clouds can contain floating or inconsistent points. The method freezes its geometry branch and trains a separate branch to predict Gaussian attributes. In particular, learned opacity allows unreliable points to contribute less to the final rendering. Rather than requiring every imperfect point to be corrected geometrically, the model can reduce the visual impact of inconsistent geometry when producing new views. [...] InfiniSplat V2 demo showing 50 input views and loaded camera poses in the sidebar, alongside a reconstructed bedroom scene with a bed, wardrobe and garden-facing windows./webresources/Blog/infinisplat-2.png "InfiniSplat V2 reconstructs 3D Gaussian scenes from multiple overlapping photographs, allowing users to explore the scene from new viewpoints.")InfiniSplat V2: Multi-View 3D Gaussian Splatting Reconstruction

Training also uses scale-aligned ground-truth cameras and target views with larger angular differences. The authors report improved rendering under large viewpoint changes. Reconstruction still depends on what the input photographs cover.

# InfiniSplat Moves from Single-Image to Multi-View 3DGS Reconstruction

Explore InfiniSplat's single-image and multi-view workflows, the code, model weights and demos available to try.

KIRI Team · Oct 16, 2026

InfiniSplat is a feed-forward reconstruction workflow for novel-view rendering from the research group ZJU3DV. V1 turns a single image into an explorable 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scene, designed to maintain more coherent spatial structure as the viewpoint changes. The updated V2 extends this workflow to multiple photographs of the same scene, reconstructing a 3D Gaussian scene that can be explored from new viewpoints.

results.content:
## Why game devs should care

Photogrammetry and per-scene 3DGS training both ask for dozens to hundreds of photos and minutes to hours of optimization for each location. InfiniSplat v2 takes a handful of overlapping shots and gives you a splat in a single inference pass. That makes it practical as a quick capture tool: scan a real corridor, café or rooftop to use as level-blockout reference, lighting and look-dev reference, or a background plate for a world-model or video pipeline. The output is a standard Gaussian `.ply`, the format that PlayCanvas/SuperSplat and the common Unity and Unreal Gaussian-splat plugins read. We haven't tested engine import ourselves yet.

## Caveats [...] ## Conclusion

InfiniSplat v2 is one of the cleaner open releases for turning a handful of photos into a Gaussian scene: real weights, a working CLI with three camera modes, COLMAP and video recipes, and a free browser demo. For game teams, it's a fast way to capture real places as splats for reference and look-dev. Register before you use it on a team project, and plan to fix the scale yourself.

—Titus

### Keep Exploring

 View All → [...] Licence isn't Apache/MIT: PRL v1.0 is free for research, education and personal use. Any company or organization project, commercial or not, internal or not, must be registered via ZJU's form before use begins. Registration is free and automatic. The DA3 backbone and the weight bundle also carry their own terms, so check them before you ship.
 Not metric: PLY coordinates are in the model's normalized RDNorm space, not world units. Expect to rescale and orient the scene by hand in your engine.
 SH0 only: the export has no view-dependent spherical harmonics, so shiny surfaces won't shift highlights as you move.
 Static scenes only: moving objects, motion blur, video cuts and large exposure changes all hurt the result. Quality depends on overlap and camera estimates.
